extraction.name: MATHVISTA : EVALUATING MATHEMATICAL REASONING OF FOUNDATION MODELS IN VISUAL CONTEXTS
extraction.description: MATHVISTA is a benchmark designed to combine challenges from diverse mathematical and visual tasks. It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). Completing these tasks requires fine-grained, deep visual understanding and compositional reasoning, which all state-of-the-art foundation models find challenging. The dataset is motivated to bridge the gap in existing benchmarks that primarily evaluate mathematical reasoning in textual contexts, overlooking the intrinsic visual nature of many mathematical problems. It offers a robust evaluation benchmark for mathematical reasoning intertwined with visual understanding, thus pushing AI assistants towards general-purpose capabilities. The benchmark covers multiple tasks and topics, incorporates diverse visual contexts and mathematical skills, offers varying levels of challenge, and provides robust evaluation settings for deterministic evaluations.
extraction.creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
extraction.citeAs: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao. MATHVISTA : EVALUATING MATHEMATICAL REASONING OF FOUNDATION MODELS IN VISUAL CONTEXTS. Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: MATHVISTA is a consolidated Mathematical reasoning benchmark in Visual contexts. It incorporates 28 existing multimodal datasets, including 9 math-targeted question answering (MathQA) datasets and 19 VQA datasets. In addition, three new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) were created to address specific gaps in logical reasoning on puzzle test diagrams, statistical reasoning on functional plots, and scientific reasoning on academic figures. IQTest comprises 228 examples requiring inductive reasoning, abstract thinking, pattern prediction, and calculations, sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms. FunctionQA, with 400 examples, emphasizes subtle visual perceptions of functional plots and algebraic reasoning. PaperQA is a novel dataset featuring questions derived from informative academic illustrations, including tables, figures, and charts from online education resources, with 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface. Each source dataset is limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation. For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were initially designed to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning (numeric answers or quantity words in questions). This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, which were then manually labeled by three expert annotators to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning, utilizing majority voting and limiting each source dataset to 400 examples, finalizing a collection of 2,739 examples. Overall, MATHVISTA consists of 6,141 examples, with 736 of them being newly curated.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset is derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). IQTest examples are sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms. PaperQA examples are sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface. VQA datasets were collected from more than 70 publicly available datasets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were initially designed to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words (as listed in §D.1) in the questions were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, though some false positive examples remained. Therefore, three expert annotators manually labeled these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning. Utilizing majority voting and limiting each source dataset to 400 examples, a collection of 2,739 examples was finalized. The MATHVISTA dataset is divided into two subsets: testmini (1,000 examples) and test (5,141 examples). A sampling strategy was adopted to ensure each source dataset is well represented in testmini and to maintain a distribution closely resembling the whole set: (1) first, randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) then, randomly sample the remaining questions for each source dataset on its proportion in the entire set. Quality checks were also conducted to address any unidentified errors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: To ensure data quality for the three new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA), all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. A two-step process was employed for consistency: initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. Discrepancies (only 6 out of 736 new questions) were resolved through discussion among the entire review team to reach a consensus. For metadata annotation, examples in MATHVISTA are annotated with information including question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context, which are accurately obtained from the details provided in the source datasets. Coarse labels of mathematical reasoning are automatically obtained from the details of the source datasets. To verify the quality of automatic annotation, expert annotators manually labeled the mathematical reasoning categories from seven candidates for 1,000 examples, using an annotation tool. The results showed 94.1% exact same set of reasoning types and 98.79% identical individual labels between automatic and human annotations, indicating high accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A custom annotation tool was developed for human annotators to label problems involving mathematical reasoning (Figure 22 in §D.2) and for annotating the three new datasets (Figure 23 in §D.3). Another GUI was used for labeling mathematical reasoning skills (Figure 24 in §D.4). Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) was used for human performance baseline evaluation and for Multimodal Bard assessment tasks.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human labeling of mathematical problems, the Fleiss Kappa score was used to conduct an inter-annotator agreement analysis among three annotators. The analysis yielded a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating a substantial level of consistency. For the three new datasets, independent annotation by three reviewers resulted in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%, with only 6 out of 736 new questions exhibiting disagreements, which were resolved through discussion. For mathematical reasoning categories, expert annotators manually labeled 1,000 examples, and the results showed 94.1% of examples from automatic and human annotations had the exact same set of reasoning types, while 98.79% of individual labels were identical, indicating high accuracy of automatic annotation.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 (for human labeling of mathematical problems and new datasets), 5 (for human performance baseline)
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: For human labeling of mathematical problems, annotators were experts. For human performance baseline, eligible human annotators must have a satisfactory annotating history, successfully pass qualification examples, and possess a high school degree or higher. Annotators who had achieved a high school diploma or higher were retained for the final analysis. For the Multimodal Bard assessment task, human workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) were used, compensated at a rate of $18 per hour.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: EasyOCR (for OCR text detection), Multimodal Bard (for image captioning)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The answer labels for the 'test' subset will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination, and an online evaluation platform will be maintained. The benchmark is part of an ongoing research process, and the maintainers are committed to maintaining the datasets, such as refining potential data noise, in response to community feedback. They are also committed to evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes natural images which may contain human attributes, as indicated by the 'Natural Image' visual context type and questions like 'What is the age gap between these two people in image?'. However, no specific sensitive human attributes are explicitly collected or discussed beyond what is visually present in the images.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: AI agents with strong mathematical reasoning capabilities in visual contexts have a wide range of real-world applications, such as solving complex problems in educational disciplines, helping analysts with logical queries about statistical data, and assisting in theorem proving and scientific discovery in advanced research fields. The benchmark aims to facilitate the development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios and evaluate the research progress of LLMs and LMMs, especially their capabilities in solving rigorous reasoning tasks. The dataset's structured categorization across grade levels (elementary school, high school, college) enriches its diversity, providing a meaningful framework for evaluating and benchmarking the practical utility and educational relevance of various models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper does not explicitly discuss data biases. However, it mentions that LLMs can suffer from unstable performance drops when using larger numbers of few-shot examples, suggesting sensitivity to bias in demonstrations, especially in the absence of visual inputs. Multimodal Bard's responses are found to contain hallucinations (49.6% of incorrect explanations), which is a major source of errors in generative foundation models.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: One limitation is the dataset coverage; while broad, there may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. The focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts, spanning specific domains like science and college-level math, necessitates a more labor-intensive process for collecting high-quality data compared to textual-only or general-purpose datasets. Thus, the scalability and generalizability of the benchmark to other domains remain a concern. Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples having annotations, and due to the heterogeneity of these sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure. The study focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent models, which is a limitation. The benchmark is challenging, with human performance reaching only 60.3% accuracy. GPT-4V still falls short of human performance by 10.4%, often struggling to understand complex figures and perform rigorous reasoning. Open-source models achieve underwhelming performance due to lack of math reasoning capabilities, text recognition, shape detection, and chart understanding. Strong text recognition abilities do not guarantee high performance on MATHVISTA, which requires comprehensive visual perception and mathematical reasoning. Self-verification in GPT-4V does not guarantee an accurate response even after multiple tries, especially for visual perception or mathematical reasoning in intricate scenarios, and is weaker for non-English tasks. GPT-4V struggles to generate correct responses when questions and user hints are ambiguous, or when the model fails to understand abstract shapes and concepts visually.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Evaluation, Benchmarking. The dataset is designed to facilitate the development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios and to evaluate the research progress of LLMs and LMMs, especially their capabilities in solving rigorous reasoning tasks. It is intended for comprehensive, quantitative evaluation of foundation models for mathematical reasoning in visual contexts. The 'testmini' subset is intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources.
